currentContext.strengths: Multi-destination model spanning the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, the Middle East and the United States, so demand redistributed away from one corridor is recaptured within the same network rather than lost to a competitor.|Depth and longevity of university relationships: more than 400 global institutions of higher education, with the top 30 university partners maintaining an average relationship tenure of over five years.|Scale of the counselling-partner network - 15,980+ registered partners including 5,389 active - with the active partner base expanding 36% during the year while applications processed per active partner continued to rise.|Compliance and process discipline as a barrier to entry: frameworks such as the UK Agent Quality Framework and British Council Accreditation raise oversight standards industry-wide and favour operators with established compliance infrastructure, with universities concentrating relationships on fewer, higher-quality partners.|Proprietary technology stack - the Central Application Management System (CAMS), the Crizac Intelligence Platform integrating application data, partner analytics and university conversion metrics, and the EduMentor AI investment - supporting AI-led error minimisation, low rejection rates and operating leverage as volumes grow.|Asset-light operating model supported by a debt-free balance sheet and healthy liquidity, allowing expansion across geographies, institutions and service offerings while maintaining financial discipline.|Demonstrated inorganic capability: a repeatable, acquisition-led market-entry model (Global Tree, Studies Planet, the Medway Educational Consultant team) that adds source-market diversity and new geographies.
currentContext.strategies: Destination diversification away from a single-corridor model: the UK contributes approximately 97% of revenue today, and management has set a calibrated, long-term goal of reducing UK reliance while scaling sustainable revenue from non-UK destinations.|Broadening source markets beyond India - FY 2025-26 was the first year in which students sourced from outside India accounted for more than half of total recruitment volumes, a direct consequence of the geographic diversification strategy.|Acquisition-led corridor entry: StudiesPlanet opened the Latin American corridor (which shows higher enrolment conversion than several established source geographies), Global Tree Careers added B2C/direct-to-student capability in India, and Medway Educational Consultants provided immediate on-ground expertise and university relationships in New Zealand, compressing the market-entry timeline.|Deliberate expansion into Southeast Asia and China, chosen for strong conversion rates and sustained middle-class demand for international education.|Sequenced destination build-out: Australia with university contracts under finalisation and entry targeted within three to six months; the United States positioned for gradual scale-up as visa and policy conditions improve; Canada under monitoring pending policy evolution; Germany and France with presence established and foundations being built; Ireland established and expanding.|Maintaining an on-ground operational presence across 10 countries to gain first-hand visibility into local student sentiment, regulatory developments and admission trends, and to adapt the sourcing mix quickly.|Building a proprietary intelligence layer as the durable moat: the Central Application Management System (CAMS) has evolved from an application-management tool into a unified intelligence framework linking partner performance analytics, university conversion trends, student quality metrics and visa outcome data, operating across descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive levels.|Positioning compliance as a competitive asset: aligning with the UK Agent Quality Framework through documented quality controls, continuous staff training and operational discipline, so that rising sector standards consolidate rather than threaten Crizac's position.|Quality-led service model for universities - screening every application for eligibility and documentation completeness before submission, providing counselling kits, documentation checklists and pre-assessment support to partners, and dedicated back-end teams per submission pipeline.|Extending the value of the platform's data beyond application processing into broader areas such as talent mobility, helping universities, employers and other ecosystem participants understand evolving student preferences, academic pathways and employability trends.
currentContext.expansion: Crizac is an asset-light, technology-enabled platform, so its expansion is footprint- and acquisition-led rather than plant-led; the Board's Report explicitly records that the Company was not engaged in any manufacturing or processing activity, that capital investment on energy conservation equipment was Nil, that it has entered into no technology agreement or collaboration, and that expenditure incurred on research and development was None. Growth in FY 2025-26 came through corporate acquisitions: the Company acquired 51.04% of the equity share capital of Global Tree Careers Private Limited (a Telangana- and Andhra Pradesh-focused overseas education and immigration advisory business), while its wholly owned UK subsidiary Crizac Ltd acquired a 51% equity stake in Studies Planet.Com Limited, England, which became a step-down subsidiary; Ucol Fze, a wholly owned subsidiary, was incorporated on 18 March 2025 under the Sharjah Publishing City Free Zone Authority in the UAE. Geographic build-out is described corridor by corridor: the United Kingdom remains the primary market at approximately 97% of revenue with the Agent Quality Framework seen as consolidating Crizac's position; New Zealand expansion was strengthened post balance sheet through the Medway team onboarding in April 2026; Ireland is established and expanding; Germany and France are active with foundations being built; Australia has university contracts under finalisation with entry targeted within three to six months; and the United States has a presence established with institutional relationships under development. On the source side, the StudiesPlanet acquisition opened the Latin American corridor - a market showing higher enrolment conversion rates than several established source geographies - and expansion into Southeast Asia and China reflects a deliberate push into markets with strong conversion and sustained middle-class demand. The Company maintains an on-ground operational presence across 10 countries. No rupee capital-expenditure quantum, capital commitment or installed capacity is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.
currentContext.mdna: Global growth is projected by the IMF at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027 - continuity rather than collapse, but below the pre-pandemic trend; for a business linked to cross-border mobility and discretionary household spend, management frames this as cautious continuity where visa certainty, value for money, speed to employment and destination diversification become more influential in student decision-making.|India's macro resilience is described as one of the clearest structural supports for outbound student demand - GDP growth of 7.8% year-on-year in Q1 FY 2025-26 and a FY 2024-25 fiscal deficit of 4.8% of GDP, better than the budgeted 4.9%.|Demographics as the long-duration demand engine: a working-age population (15-64) of roughly 988 million, about 68% of the total, expected to peak near 69% by 2030, with a median age of about 28 years - the primary cohort generating demand for internationally recognised degrees.|Middle-class expansion: India's middle class is projected to grow from around 430 million individuals in 2020-21 to roughly 715 million by 2030-31 and to exceed one billion by 2047, with middle-class and affluent consumers potentially accounting for more than 90% of consumer spending by the mid-2030s; total overseas education spend by Indian students is estimated at around GBP 50 billion.|Market size backdrop: the global education market was valued at around USD 7.3 trillion in 2025 and may rise to USD 10 trillion by 2030; digital education alone was worth about USD 404 billion in 2025 and may rise to nearly USD 850 billion by 2030.|The addressable services layer: the global study abroad agency market stood at USD 22.7 billion in 2023 and is projected to reach about USD 41.3 billion by 2032, covering counselling, course selection, application support, document checks, visa guidance and pre-departure support - the layer Crizac operates in.|Structural mobility growth: the number of students studying outside their home country has tripled over two decades, from around 2.1 million to nearly 7.3 million, with spending patterns diversifying into shorter bridging programmes, English-language preparation and professional qualification pathways.|Demand resilience: because families are paying for a possibility and a different labour market rather than only a degree, demand tends to hold up even when macro conditions tighten, though students and parents become more selective.|Destination-mix shift rather than demand destruction: changes in immigration and visa policy redistribute student demand across destinations, which favours multi-corridor platforms; in the US, recent visa measures contributed to a 17% decline in new enrolments and an overall 1% dip in fall 2025 against a base of approximately 1.1 million international students in 2023-24, with industry forecasts suggesting the moderation may be temporary.|New Zealand as a policy-backed growth destination: international student enrolments have more than doubled from 41,400 in 2022 to 92,580 in 2025, including 11% growth in the latest year, with the Government's Going for Growth plan targeting 105,000 international students by 2027 and 119,000 by 2034.|University behaviour: institutions are concentrating recruitment on partners that demonstrate consistency, reliability and long-term commitment to quality, shifting emphasis from volume to student quality, compliance and outcomes.|Latin America contributes higher enrolment conversion rates than several of Crizac's established source geographies, and its contribution to enrolments is expected to increase progressively as StudiesPlanet integrates.|Australia: university contracts under finalisation, with market entry targeted within three to six months.|United States: presence established with institutional relationships under development, positioned for gradual scale-up as visa and policy conditions become more supportive.

risks.risk: Immigration, visa and education-policy change in destination countries
risks.note: The MD&A risk table names this first: stricter visa regulations, work-permit restrictions or immigration policy changes in key destination countries may impact student mobility and enrolment volumes. The BRSR material-issues table repeats it as 'Education Policies', citing regulatory changes in the UK or USA regarding international student enrollment and compliance issues with agencies in India, and states it may impact the Company's business and revenue from operations. Because Crizac earns from placements, a policy shift in one corridor translates directly into volumes; mitigation is a diversified destination portfolio spanning the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and the US plus close monitoring of policy developments.

The Board's risk-management commentary explicitly lists 'destination concentration' among the exposures a multi-jurisdictional education platform faces, and the MD&A risk table flags University Partner Concentration Risk - dependence on a limited number of institutions may impact revenues if partnerships change. Mitigation is continuous expansion of the university network across geographies and disciplines and deepening of existing institutional relationships. Structurally, exports are 100% of turnover and revenue is generated from a single activity (education consultancy services), so there is no domestic or segment offset if a corridor or a large institutional relationship turns.

Inconsistent service quality or non-compliance by counselling partners could affect student outcomes and institutional reputation - a direct threat in a business whose value proposition to universities is application quality and compliance rigour. Because the network is large and third-party, control depends on structured onboarding, adherence to the UK Agent Quality Framework, application quality controls, AI-led error-minimisation tools, performance monitoring, compliance checks and training programmes rather than direct employment.

risks.risk: Technology platform, AI/algorithmic and data-privacy exposure
risks.note: The proprietary platform is central to business operations, so system outages, technology disruptions or infrastructure failures directly interrupt service delivery. Layered on this, errors, biases or failures in AI-driven screening, matching or decision-support tools may affect application quality, student outcomes or institutional trust - a risk the Company created for itself by making AI a control mechanism rather than only a commercial capability. The BRSR names Data Privacy as its first material issue: the Company is subject to stringent data protection laws, in particular the EU General Data Protection Regulations, and states it cannot assure that a breach will not occur or that it can successfully mitigate one, with potential additional costs, loss of personal data and legal proceedings that may adversely affect revenue.

The Company completed two strategic acquisitions during FY 2025-26 and states it has an active pipeline for further inorganic growth. Multiple acquisitions within a short timeframe may create challenges in aligning technology systems, compliance standards, partner quality frameworks and operational processes across acquired entities - which matters more than usual here because compliance consistency is the moat, so a weakly integrated entity imports reputational and regulatory risk into the group.

Fluctuations in currency exchange rates, particularly INR-GBP volatility given the significance of sterling-denominated university payouts, may affect realisations and reported financial performance. With exports at 100% of turnover and the UK the dominant destination, the currency exposure is structural rather than incidental; mitigation is limited to monitoring, prudent treasury practices and geographic diversification of revenue streams.

The BRSR discloses an attrition rate for permanent employees of 33.5% in Fiscal 2025-26, up from 28.74% in Fiscal 2025 and 20.67% in Fiscal 2024 - a rising trend in a 356-permanent-employee organisation whose output is relationship management and application assessment. The BRSR separately identifies Employee Salary as a material risk: competition for skilled and semi-skilled employees in India is pushing wages up fast, the Company may need to raise compensation to retain quality staff, and a significant long-term increase in employee benefit expense could reduce profitability and impact growth prospects.

risks.risk: Intra-group revenue structure and the absence of a formal inter-company arrangement
risks.note: The BRSR discloses that Crizac's two key customer entities are its own wholly owned subsidiaries, Crizac Ltd (UK) and Ucol Fze, so essentially all turnover is booked against related parties. The material-issues table raises this as a Conflict of Interest risk: the Company and both subsidiaries are in the same line of business, and while the Company asserts no conflict arises because they are wholly owned, it acknowledges there is no formal agreement, arrangement or memorandum of understanding governing the relationship (the disclosure is truncated at this point in the bundle). Transfer-pricing, arm's-length and governance scrutiny therefore sit on an informal footing.

one-line thesis: Crizac delivered strong FY26 growth (22.7% revenue, 41% PAT) driven by geographic expansion and acquisitions, with Q4 margin expansion fueled by FX gains; the key shift is structural diversification away from UK dependency toward Australia, NZ, and LATAM, creating resilience against visa policy shocks and deepening platform moats via scale and AI.
financial scorecard: revenue: 10,422M (+22.7% YoY); EBITDA: 2,824M (+31% YoY, margin 27%); PAT (rptd): 2,191M (+41% YoY, margin 20.5%); PAT (normalized): ~2,063M (excl. INR 128M FX gain); order book: Not disclosed; net debt: Net cash of 4,674M (debt-free)
guidance: revenue growth: 15-17% FY27 (implied); margin: EBITDA margin expected to stabilize near 25-27% post-FX normalization; order inflow: No specific guidance; capex/commissioning: INR 2.5M over 5 years for EduMentor AI platform; no other capex disclosed
segment / subsidiary detail: UK: 97% of revenue (targeting <60% by FY28); LATAM: via StudiesPlanet acquisition; India: <50% of student origin (down from >50%); New Zealand: fully operationalized via Medway team; Australia: in negotiation phase with 300+ universities; Germany/France: expanding; China/Southeast Asia: higher conversion rates (20%)
growth verticals / optionality: Australia (next 3-6 months), US (300+ university partnerships secured), Canada (policy-dependent), EU expansion; B2C services via Global Tree Careers; EduMentor AI platform for conversion optimization
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA margin expansion to 27% FY26 driven by operating leverage; Q4 margin (24%) inflated by INR 128M FX gain (pound strengthened from 110 to 125); normalized EBITDA margin target: 25-27%; gross margin improved to 32.5% (from 29.5%) due to FX, not structural mix change
capex / expansion: INR 2.5M over 5 years for EduMentor AI project; no other capex disclosed; asset-light model
capital allocation: Dividend payout increased to 64% (from 40% commitment); net cash position of INR 4,674M supports future M&A; no share buybacks or debt used; prioritizing strategic acquisitions over buybacks
risks & watch-items: UK visa policy shifts (e.g., graduate visa reduced to 18 months — already priced in); geopolitical instability in Middle East; Australia/US entry delays due to university contract negotiations; FX volatility; regulatory burden (Agent Quality Framework) favors incumbents but increases compliance cost
management quality / tone: Confident, strategic, and disciplined; emphasized platform moats, geographic diversification, and regulatory tailwinds; avoided firm FY27 guidance due to geopolitical uncertainty but signaled intent to grow 15-17%; tone on acquisitions was deliberate and execution-focused
non-obvious takeaways: Agent network growth (5,389) is highly fragmented — low-volume agents contribute significantly, making per-agent productivity metrics misleading; FX gain of INR 128M in Q4 materially boosted PAT — normalized PAT was ~INR 622M; the 97% UK concentration is being actively dismantled via Australia/NZ, not just passive shift

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: revenue growth: 15-17% FY27 (implied); margin: EBITDA margin expected to stabilize near 25-27% post-FX normalization; order inflow: No specific guidance; capex/commissioning: INR 2.5M over 5 years for EduMentor AI platform; no other capex disclosed

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: Australia (next 3-6 months), US (300+ university partnerships secured), Canada (policy-dependent), EU expansion; B2C services via Global Tree Careers; EduMentor AI platform for conversion optimization

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Global growth is projected by the IMF at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027 - continuity rather than collapse, but below the pre-pandemic trend; for a business linked to cross-border mobility and discretionary household spend, management frames this as cautious continuity where visa certainty, value for money, speed to employment and destination diversification become more influential in student decision-making.
- India's macro resilience is described as one of the clearest structural supports for outbound student demand - GDP growth of 7.8% year-on-year in Q1 FY 2025-26 and a FY 2024-25 fiscal deficit of 4.8% of GDP, better than the budgeted 4.9%.
- Demographics as the long-duration demand engine: a working-age population (15-64) of roughly 988 million, about 68% of the total, expected to peak near 69% by 2030, with a median age of about 28 years - the primary cohort generating demand for internationally recognised degrees.
- Middle-class expansion: India's middle class is projected to grow from around 430 million individuals in 2020-21 to roughly 715 million by 2030-31 and to exceed one billion by 2047, with middle-class and affluent consumers potentially accounting for more than 90% of consumer spending by the mid-2030s; total overseas education spend by Indian students is estimated at around GBP 50 billion.
- Market size backdrop: the global education market was valued at around USD 7.3 trillion in 2025 and may rise to USD 10 trillion by 2030; digital education alone was worth about USD 404 billion in 2025 and may rise to nearly USD 850 billion by 2030.
- The addressable services layer: the global study abroad agency market stood at USD 22.7 billion in 2023 and is projected to reach about USD 41.3 billion by 2032, covering counselling, course selection, application support, document checks, visa guidance and pre-departure support - the layer Crizac operates in.
- Structural mobility growth: the number of students studying outside their home country has tripled over two decades, from around 2.1 million to nearly 7.3 million, with spending patterns diversifying into shorter bridging programmes, English-language preparation and professional qualification pathways.
- Demand resilience: because families are paying for a possibility and a different labour market rather than only a degree, demand tends to hold up even when macro conditions tighten, though students and parents become more selective.
- Destination-mix shift rather than demand destruction: changes in immigration and visa policy redistribute student demand across destinations, which favours multi-corridor platforms; in the US, recent visa measures contributed to a 17% decline in new enrolments and an overall 1% dip in fall 2025 against a base of approximately 1.1 million international students in 2023-24, with industry forecasts suggesting the moderation may be temporary.
- New Zealand as a policy-backed growth destination: international student enrolments have more than doubled from 41,400 in 2022 to 92,580 in 2025, including 11% growth in the latest year, with the Government's Going for Growth plan targeting 105,000 international students by 2027 and 119,000 by 2034.
- University behaviour: institutions are concentrating recruitment on partners that demonstrate consistency, reliability and long-term commitment to quality, shifting emphasis from volume to student quality, compliance and outcomes.
- Latin America contributes higher enrolment conversion rates than several of Crizac's established source geographies, and its contribution to enrolments is expected to increase progressively as StudiesPlanet integrates.
- Australia: university contracts under finalisation, with market entry targeted within three to six months.
- United States: presence established with institutional relationships under development, positioned for gradual scale-up as visa and policy conditions become more supportive.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: EBITDA margin expansion to 27% FY26 driven by operating leverage; Q4 margin (24%) inflated by INR 128M FX gain (pound strengthened from 110 to 125); normalized EBITDA margin target: 25-27%; gross margin improved to 32.5% (from 29.5%) due to FX, not structural mix change

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Dividend payout increased to 64% (from 40% commitment); net cash position of INR 4,674M supports future M&A; no share buybacks or debt used; prioritizing strategic acquisitions over buybacks

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Crizac is an asset-light, technology-enabled platform, so its expansion is footprint- and acquisition-led rather than plant-led; the Board's Report explicitly records that the Company was not engaged in any manufacturing or processing activity, that capital investment on energy conservation equipment was Nil, that it has entered into no technology agreement or collaboration, and that expenditure incurred on research and development was None. Growth in FY 2025-26 came through corporate acquisitions: the Company acquired 51.04% of the equity share capital of Global Tree Careers Private Limited (a Telangana- and Andhra Pradesh-focused overseas education and immigration advisory business), while its wholly owned UK subsidiary Crizac Ltd acquired a 51% equity stake in Studies Planet.Com Limited, England, which became a step-down subsidiary; Ucol Fze, a wholly owned subsidiary, was incorporated on 18 March 2025 under the Sharjah Publishing City Free Zone Authority in the UAE. Geographic build-out is described corridor by corridor: the United Kingdom remains the primary market at approximately 97% of revenue with the Agent Quality Framework seen as consolidating Crizac's position; New Zealand expansion was strengthened post balance sheet through the Medway team onboarding in April 2026; Ireland is established and expanding; Germany and France are active with foundations being built; Australia has university contracts under finalisation with entry targeted within three to six months; and the United States has a presence established with institutional relationships under development. On the source side, the StudiesPlanet acquisition opened the Latin American corridor - a market showing higher enrolment conversion rates than several established source geographies - and expansion into Southeast Asia and China reflects a deliberate push into markets with strong conversion and sustained middle-class demand. The Company maintains an on-ground operational presence across 10 countries. No rupee capital-expenditure quantum, capital commitment or installed capacity is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident, strategic, and disciplined; emphasized platform moats, geographic diversification, and regulatory tailwinds; avoided firm FY27 guidance due to geopolitical uncertainty but signaled intent to grow 15-17%; tone on acquisitions was deliberate and execution-focused

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Multi-destination model spanning the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, the Middle East and the United States, so demand redistributed away from one corridor is recaptured within the same network rather than lost to a competitor.
- Depth and longevity of university relationships: more than 400 global institutions of higher education, with the top 30 university partners maintaining an average relationship tenure of over five years.
- Scale of the counselling-partner network - 15,980+ registered partners including 5,389 active - with the active partner base expanding 36% during the year while applications processed per active partner continued to rise.
- Compliance and process discipline as a barrier to entry: frameworks such as the UK Agent Quality Framework and British Council Accreditation raise oversight standards industry-wide and favour operators with established compliance infrastructure, with universities concentrating relationships on fewer, higher-quality partners.
- Proprietary technology stack - the Central Application Management System (CAMS), the Crizac Intelligence Platform integrating application data, partner analytics and university conversion metrics, and the EduMentor AI investment - supporting AI-led error minimisation, low rejection rates and operating leverage as volumes grow.
- Asset-light operating model supported by a debt-free balance sheet and healthy liquidity, allowing expansion across geographies, institutions and service offerings while maintaining financial discipline.
- Demonstrated inorganic capability: a repeatable, acquisition-led market-entry model (Global Tree, Studies Planet, the Medway Educational Consultant team) that adds source-market diversity and new geographies.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: UK visa policy shifts (e.g., graduate visa reduced to 18 months — already priced in); geopolitical instability in Middle East; Australia/US entry delays due to university contract negotiations; FX volatility; regulatory burden (Agent Quality Framework) favors incumbents but increases compliance cost

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Agent network growth (5,389) is highly fragmented — low-volume agents contribute significantly, making per-agent productivity metrics misleading; FX gain of INR 128M in Q4 materially boosted PAT — normalized PAT was ~INR 622M; the 97% UK concentration is being actively dismantled via Australia/NZ, not just passive shift

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Destination diversification away from a single-corridor model: the UK contributes approximately 97% of revenue today, and management has set a calibrated, long-term goal of reducing UK reliance while scaling sustainable revenue from non-UK destinations.
- Broadening source markets beyond India - FY 2025-26 was the first year in which students sourced from outside India accounted for more than half of total recruitment volumes, a direct consequence of the geographic diversification strategy.

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Leadership change] Christopher Nagle steps down as Chief Executive Officer of the UK entity while remaining a Director there, and takes the role of Non-Executive Director and Chairman of the Indian holding company, providing board-level oversight while executive management retains day-to-day responsibility.
- [Regulation] Global mobility is described as increasingly policy-sensitive: stricter visa regimes, the UK's AQF and BCA compliance requirements, and Canada/US tightening "redirecting demand towards UK, Ireland, Germany and New Zealand".
- [Accounting change] Depreciation method revised from Written Down Value (WDV) to Straight Line Method (SLM) with effect from April 01, 2026, accounted for prospectively.
- [Corporate structure] Holding company Crizac Limited (India) with subsidiaries Crizac Ltd (United Kingdom), Global Tree Careers Private Limited (51.04% majority stake), UCOL FZE, Studies Planet.com Ltd and step-down subsidiary Inova Consultancy Limited.
- [Shareholding] Promoter and Promoter Group hold 79.9% as on 30th June 2026; marquee investors named include Carnelian Funds, Aryabhata India Fund (Abakkus), India Equity Fund, 360 ONE Funds, Allianz Global Fund and ICICI Prudential Fund.
